title: Critical moments and where to spend your time
summary: Recognise the positions that decide the game and invest your clock there; play routine moves quickly.

steps.question: Which of these positions deserves a long think?
choices: You can trade rooks into a pawn endgame
The only legal recapture after an exchange
Move 6 of your well-known opening line
steps.explain: A pawn endgame is irreversible and its evaluation is concrete (win/draw/loss). Recaptures with no alternative and memorised theory should be fast.

steps.question: Rook endgame, White to move: is this a critical moment?
choices: Yes: 1.Rxd8 would trade into a lost pawn ending against the outside passer, while 1.Ra1 keeps a defensible rook ending
No, rook endgames are always drawn
steps.explain: Exactly the kind of decision that deserves your time: one move changes the result. Engine check: 1.Ra1 about -1.3, 1.Rxd8 about -8.5.

steps.question: You are playing 90 min + 30 s. On move 14 you have used 65 minutes in a quiet position. What is the most likely problem?
choices: Over-checking routine moves; you will reach the critical moments short of time
Nothing; using time early is always good
steps.explain: Time spent early on routine decisions is missing later in the critical positions. Diagnose it in your game reviews: where did the minutes go?

steps.question: Your opponent makes a move you did not expect. What is the best reaction?
choices: Treat it as a potential critical moment: check his threats and your forcing replies before continuing your plan
Play your prepared plan quickly anyway
steps.explain: Surprises are a signal: the position may have changed character. Ask "What does he want?" (prophylactic thinking) before resuming.

steps.question: In time trouble, which technique is recommended?
choices: Simplify, make safe moves, use the opponent's time to think, and avoid long forcing lines you cannot verify
Stop recording and play instantly in every position
steps.explain: KB time-management guidance: keep the position under control, trade when ahead, avoid unverifiable complications, and keep a reserve when there is no increment.

steps.md: **Retrieval check.** Name four signals of a critical moment. What is the classical "move 15" time guideline? After your next long game, mark the two most critical moments and check how much time you spent on each.

sources: Kotov, Think Like a Grandmaster (1971), time trouble
Dvoretsky & Yusupov, Secrets of Chess Training (Edition Olms, 1996)
